content.p: Between 7 November and early December 1936, thousands of prisoners were taken out of the jails of besieged Madrid in convoys that were officially transfers to another place of detention. Many never arrived. They were shot in open country near the villages of Paracuellos de Jarama and Torrejón de Ardoz and buried in mass graves. The Edinburgh historian Julius Ruiz wrote a 2015 book on the episode, which his university describes as examining the most polemical atrocity of the Spanish Civil War; he puts the dead at about 2,500.

The killings happened on the watch of a 21-year-old Communist, Santiago Carrillo, who was responsible for public order in the city. He lived to the age of 97, became a leader of the Spanish Communist Party and played a part in the transition to democracy after Franco's death, and he died in 2012 still denying any involvement. Whether he, the Soviet advisers in Madrid, a revolutionary tribunal or the Republican government bear the main blame is the question that has divided historians ever since.
content.h2: A besieged city and a fear of traitors
content.p: In early November 1936 Franco's forces were closing on Madrid. The Republican government of Francisco Largo Caballero left for Valencia, and an emergency body, the Junta de Defensa de Madrid, took charge of the capital under General José Miaja. Behind the lines the city was gripped by a fear that a clandestine pro-Franco "fifth column" waited to strike from within. Ruiz's reviewers describe how this fear grew as the front approached. By the first days of November about 10,000 political prisoners were in Madrid's jails, and a further 8,798 people were sheltering in foreign embassies, according to the review of Ruiz's book in the Abraham Lincoln Brigade Archives' journal.

The killing of prisoners did not begin that month. The same review notes a series of "sacas", the Spanish word for the removal of prisoners from a jail to be killed, that had been rising around Madrid through the autumn, and says complaints from the British embassy about arrests and violence were brushed aside. Ruiz argues that Paracuellos was therefore not exceptional but the peak of a wider "Red Terror" in the capital, in which, according to the Edinburgh summary of his work, at least 8,000 people were murdered after the failed military rising of July 1936.

The press of the time added to the mood. A Spanish website that treats the killings as communist crimes quotes left-wing newspapers of the period calling for prisoners to be shot. It cites a Madrid daily's call on 3 November 1936 to execute more than 100,000 camouflaged fascists, in jails and elsewhere, so that no fifth columnist survived. Those quotations come from a partisan site and are given here as its claims about what the newspapers printed.

A Spanish review of Ruiz's book, which sets out the sequence as the author describes it, says that between 7 November and 3 December 1936 there were 33 sacas. 23 of them ended with the collective killing of everyone taken out. La Ibéria, a Spanish site, says most of the prisoners came from the Cárcel Modelo, though convoys also left San Antón, Ventas and Porlier jails. It puts the end of the killings on 4 December, says the prisoners were told they were being moved elsewhere and that the orders carried the letterhead of the Dirección General de Seguridad, in many cases with the signature of Carrillo's delegate, Segundo Serrano Poncela.

The same review says that prisoners were loaded onto double-decker city buses and driven out to the villages, where they were shot and put into large common graves in the municipality of Paracuellos de Jarama and on one occasion at Torrejón de Ardoz. A second Spanish site, which publishes material from a pro-Franco point of view, describes buses arriving at the Cárcel Modelo between nine and ten on the morning of 7 November, victims being tied together and led to pits dug beforehand, and about 200 gravediggers recruited from nearby towns, whom it describes as alleged fascists. That account is the website's own, not an official record. It also relates that a local teenager, Ricardo Aresté, son of Paracuellos's mayor, saw around eight that morning three buses surrounded by trucks of militiamen and prisoners with bound hands being shot on the plain; in a 1983 talk with the historian Ian Gibson, the site says, Aresté said he could not forget the spectacle.

The peak came at the start. According to the review in The Volunteer, some 650 prisoners were shot on 7 and 8 November alone, and killings of prisoners fell sharply in the months after the autumn of 1936.

The figures depend heavily on who is counting. Ruiz, in the summaries of his work, gives 2,500 for the massacres at Paracuellos and Torrejón de Ardoz. Two Spanish websites that frame the killings as communist crimes give much higher numbers: generalfranco.com writes of between 5,000 and 7,000 bodies in the Paracuellos graves and, elsewhere in its text, of about 5,000 killed between 7 November and 3 December; La Ibéria says between 5,000 and 8,000, depending on the source. The generalisimofranco.com site quotes the historian Ramón Salas Larrazábal as saying that about 8,000 people died in Madrid in November and December and that around 7,000 were killed while Carrillo held responsibility. The sites do not reconcile their numbers with Ruiz's lower one. The 2,500 count is, however, the one used in the descriptions of Ruiz's book by his university and by a Spanish bookseller's listing.

The websites also stress that children were among the dead. generalfranco.com reports 276 minors killed, naming the youngest as 13-year-old Samuel Ruiz Navarro, and says that of nearly 1,000 identified bodies most showed no sign of a finishing shot. La Ibéria speaks of about 250 children. Both numbers come from partisan sites and are not confirmed by the academic summaries.

The sources also disagree about who the victims were. La Ibéria says their one shared feature was their Catholic faith, and lists officials, soldiers, students, clergy and civilians accused of being "fascists" by revolutionary committees. Ruiz's work, in the words of its publishers, treats them as political prisoners held by the Republic and killed as suspected members of a fifth column, a clandestine organisation that he describes as imaginary.
content.h2: The man in charge of public order
content.p: On 6 November 1936, the day before the first convoy, Carrillo, then of the Unified Socialist Youth, took over the Junta's public order portfolio, according to La Ibéria. The site says that jails and prisoner transport fell under his authority, and that the Norwegian consul Félix Schlayer warned him on 7 November of what was happening, without any change. According to generalisimofranco.com, Carrillo's memoirs describe his job as the fight against the fifth column. He denied involvement for the rest of his life. In a 1983 interview with Gibson, quoted by generalisimofranco.com, he said the name Paracuellos had meant nothing to him at the time and that he had not known the place existed.

La Ibéria concludes that documents and the testimony of diplomats, priests and survivors place his responsibility, at least political and moral, beyond doubt. That is the view of a polemical outlet. Ruiz, a professional historian, is more specific and more qualified. A blog review of his book quotes him as writing that the young leader did not order the atrocity but gave the logistical and political support that allowed it, and that the same could be said of other members of Miaja's Junta. The Largo Caballero government, the same review says, did not order the killings; its responsibility was one of omission and cover-up, and it stopped the executions only under heavy domestic and international pressure.

The Edinburgh summary of Ruiz's book places him between two camps. Ruiz rejects two opposing readings. One, from writers he labels right-wing "revisionists" such as César Vidal, treats Paracuellos as proof that the Republic committed Soviet-style genocide. The other, which the summary attributes to the left-wing historian Paul Preston and his book The Spanish Holocaust, holds that the NKVD, the Soviet secret police, bore chief responsibility.

His own conclusion, repeated across the reviews, is that the perpetrators were chiefly members of the CPIP, the Provincial Committee of Public Investigation, which the Edinburgh summary calls an "all-leftist" revolutionary tribunal and the Spanish review a Popular Front revolutionary tribunal created in August 1936 by the director general of security. It had, in his reading, practised the same methods well before NKVD agents reached Republican Spain, and its work was backed not only by Carrillo but by the Republican government. The Soviets, he argues, were influenced by what Madrid did rather than the reverse, and Paracuellos fed Stalin's own fears of a fifth column that fed into the Great Terror of 1937 and 1938. In a line quoted by The Volunteer he writes: "Spanish Communists did not need their Soviet comrades to tell them to act brutally against the internal enemy." He also says the blame placed on the Soviets grew out of propaganda that appeared after the killings.

The Spanish review of the book summarises Ruiz as seeing neither disorder nor spontaneity: the policing bodies of the besieged capital picked out the prisoners and, in time, killed them, with a cold if sometimes erratic logistics. The Volunteer's reviewer describes the same argument differently: the murders, he writes, were unorganised and chaotic, though not surprising given the autumn's repression. The Spanish review cites the journalist Jorge Martínez Reverte for documentary evidence that by early November prisoners were already being classified, with a category of fascists and dangerous elements marked for immediate execution while covering the responsibility of those involved. Sanabria, reviewing Ruiz's wider study of the terror, says it is built on archives and periodicals and leans heavily on the Franco regime's own post-war investigation, the Causa General, whose slant Ruiz acknowledges while defending its use because it holds Republican documents that might otherwise have been lost.

The partisan sites hold a harder view. generalisimofranco.com asserts that the Comintern agent Mikhail Koltsov ordered all prisoners in Madrid's jails shot on 6 November, and calls Carrillo a perpetrator of genocide. These are the website's assertions, not findings from the academic reviews, which report Ruiz's conclusion that the NKVD had little influence over the CPIP at the time.

La Ibéria links the killings to a second event. On 8 December 1936 a French embassy mail aircraft, a Potez 54 flying from Madrid to Toulouse, was brought down over Pastrana in Guadalajara. Aboard was a Swiss delegate of the International Red Cross, Dr Georges Henny, who the site says was carrying a dossier on the killings of prisoners, intended for the League of Nations. The Ministry of War first said the aircraft had been attacked by fascist aviation; the site says it was soon found to have been downed by two Republican Polikarpov I-15 fighters flown by Soviet pilots. It says three people were hurt, among them the French journalist Louis Delaprée, who died soon after, and quotes him as having written that the attack was ordered by Alexander Orlov, the NKVD chief in Spain. This is one outlet's account, and no other saved source covers it.

The Volunteer's reviewer describes the opposition within the Republican camp. Melchor Rodríguez, an anarchist, was appointed inspector general of the prison service on 9 November 1936 and, according to the review, tried without success to end the Paracuellos operation in early November before later succeeding, supported by figures such as the Basque nationalist minister Manuel de Irujo. Ruiz, the reviewer says, concludes that the government never acted itself to stop the killings while they were happening, which left it partly complicit. The generalisimofranco.com site says the last convoy ordered by Serrano Poncela took place on 3 December and that Rodríguez then barred further removals and expelled the rear-guard militiamen from the jails.
content.h2: Silence, memory and the continuing argument
content.p: La Ibéria says the Republican government silenced the killings from the start and that official propaganda blamed them on "fascist provocations". It adds that Franco's regime afterwards treated them as proof of "red terror", while memory of the victims faded in the decades that followed. The Edinburgh summary records one measure of the topic's continuing public pull in Spain: Ruiz's book was serialised in the national daily El Mundo in the autumn of 2015. Ruiz's earlier Spanish-language monograph on Madrid in 1936 was prize-winning, according to Sanabria's review. generalfranco.com calls the Paracuellos graves the largest of the war's repression on both sides, and complains that victims' families do not know where their relatives lie.

The central questions have not been closed. The toll varies by a factor of two or more depending on the author, and responsibility is placed on a revolutionary tribunal, on Carrillo and the Junta, on the government in Valencia, on Soviet agents, or on some combination. The outline is not in dispute: prisoners were removed from Madrid's jails on written orders, driven out of the city, and shot in the countryside, over about four weeks, and the killings fell away once the convoys were halted in early December 1936.
